hints: Focus on what paired really means, every orbital up to the valence shell must be full with two opposite-spin electrons and no half-filled orbitals left.
Write out the outer shell for each atom, Ba ends in $6s^2$, while Br ends in $4p^5$, S in $3p^4$ and Si in $3p^2$.
Apply Hund's rule to the p-subshells to count unpaired electrons, then spot which outer $s^2$ configuration leaves nothing unpaired.
walkthrough:
**Understand paired in a ground-state atom**

All electrons paired means there are zero unpaired electrons. Every occupied orbital holds two electrons, and Hund's rule gives no singly occupied p or d orbitals.

Rule to use:
$$\text{unpaired} = 0 \text{ means all subshells are either full or empty}$$

**Write the valence configurations**

Let us look just at the outer shells, since inner noble gas cores are already fully paired.

$$\text{Ba (Z=56): [Xe]} \, 6s^2$$
$$\text{Br (Z=35): [Ar]} \, 3d^{10}4s^24p^5$$
$$\text{S (Z=16): [Ne]} \, 3s^23p^4$$
$$\text{Si (Z=14): [Ne]} \, 3s^23p^2$$

**Count unpaired electrons with Hund's rule**

An $s^2$ is one full orbital, so paired. A $p^5$ has one unpaired, a $p^4$ has two unpaired, and a $p^2$ has two unpaired.

$$p^2: \uparrow \, \uparrow \, \_ \quad p^4: \uparrow\downarrow \, \uparrow \, \uparrow \quad p^5: \uparrow\downarrow \, \uparrow\downarrow \, \uparrow$$
Only Ba with a complete $[Xe]$ core plus full $6s^2$ has every electron in a pair.

options.A: Ba is correct. Its configuration is $[Xe]6s^2$. The xenon core is all paired and the $6s$ orbital holds a full pair, so there are zero unpaired electrons.
options.B: Br is not correct. $4p^5$ means two p orbitals are full but the third has a single electron, so there is one unpaired electron. Students who only check that $4s^2$ is paired often miss the half-filled p orbital.
options.C: S is not correct. $3p^4$ gives one paired p orbital plus two singly occupied p orbitals by Hund's rule, so two unpaired electrons. The trap is thinking an even number of p electrons must mean all paired.
options.D: Si is not correct. $3p^2$ places one electron in two separate p orbitals with parallel spins, so two unpaired electrons. It is a classic Hund's rule example of unpaired electrons in a Group 14 atom.
